a: Ignatius, also called Theophorus
p: Every letter opens with the same second name: Theophorus, 'God-bearer'.
b: Greek Theophoros, 'God-bearer'. Lake's footnote at Ignatius to the Ephesians 1:0 gives the story told in the third-century Acts of Ignatius: asked who Theophorus is, Ignatius answers, 'He who has Christ in his heart.' See the note at Ignatius to the Romans 1:0.

a: Philadelphia of Asia
p: A city of Lydia in the Roman province of Asia, the Philadelphia of Revelation 3.
b: Lightfoot notes that several cities bore the name. The foundation of this one is 'distinctly ascribed' to Attalus II of Pergamum, called Philadelphus (159-138 BC), yet Lightfoot adds 'we may be tempted to suspect an error', since John the Lydian, a sixth-century writer from the city, said Egyptians founded it, which would point to Ptolemy Philadelphus. The city lay at the foot of the Tmolus mountains on the road from the Maeander valley to Smyrna. Strabo, he says, describes earthquakes so constant that most people lived in the countryside, and the city was among those thrown down under Tiberius (Tacitus, Annals 2.47). The risen Christ's letter to 'the angel of the church in Philadelphia' (Revelation 3:7-13) is the earliest notice of a church there.

a: the suffering of our Lord
p: Greek pathos, 'suffering', the word behind 'the Passion'; set beside the resurrection.
b: Greek agalliōmenē en tō pathei tou kyriou hēmōn adiakritōs. Lightfoot reads the greeting as a quiet answer to those who said Christ only seemed to suffer: 'The Docetism is tacitly reproved in the opening salutation', where the church rejoices in the Passion 'without wavering' and is firm in the resurrection. Lake ties 'in his resurrection' to 'fully assured'; Lightfoot thinks it is 'perhaps best taken' with 'rejoices', so that the church rejoices in both the suffering and the resurrection. The Plain English Translation follows Lake.
orig: ἐν τῷ πάθει τοῦ κυρίου ἡμῶν ἀδιακρίτως

a: which is eternal and lasting joy
p: The Greek 'which' could point back to the blood or to the church.
b: Greek hētis estin chara aiōnios kai paramonos. The relative is feminine, like 'joy'. Lightfoot takes it of 'the blood of Jesus Christ', the gender 'attracted' to chara: the blood, truly shed, 'is the source of all abiding joy'. Lake's English agrees ('the blood of Jesus Christ, which is eternal and abiding joy'). Zahn, Lightfoot reports, referred it to the whole clause about the church rejoicing; Lightfoot finds the intervening 'which' (the church) an 'insuperable objection'.
orig: ἥτις ἐστὶν χαρὰ αἰώνιος καὶ παράμονος

a: above all if they are one with the overseer
p: Ignatius's greeting holds 'above all' for those at one with the overseer, elders and deacons.
b:
Greek malista ean en heni ōsin syn tō episkopō. 'They' are the Philadelphian Christians: Lightfoot notes the third person is kept because the address is not yet over (compare 2 John 1 and 2 John 4). The words limit the greeting: it is meant 'above all' for those united with their leaders. The same condition runs through the letter (3:2; 7:1-2; 8:1).

Episkopos is 'overseer', the word behind 'bishop', as in the site's Philippians 1:1 and 1 Timothy 3:1. Ignatius knows one overseer in each city, with a council of elders and deacons; when that pattern took hold, and whether it binds the churches, is asked on the cards at Acts 20:28, Philippians 1:1 and 1 Timothy 3.
orig: μάλιστα ἐὰν ἐν ἑνὶ ὦσιν σὺν τῷ ἐπισκόπῳ

a: appointed in keeping with the mind of Jesus Christ
t: Appointed by people, made firm by Christ
p: Lightfoot: 'appointed' is the human choice; Christ then confirms them by his Spirit.
b: Greek apodedeigmenois en gnōmē Iēsou Christou, hous kata to idion thelēma estērixen ... tō hagiō autou pneumati. Lightfoot: the participle 'refers to the nomination or election by the human agents—whether the congregation or the officers of the Church', and 'Christ confirmed and established in their office the persons so appointed through human agency by the gift of His Holy Spirit; where τὸ ἴδιον θέλημα is opposed to the ἀπόδειξις of man.' 'In keeping with the mind' (en gnōmē) is 'with the approval of', as Ignatius to the Ephesians 3:2.

a: from himself or through human beings
t: Not from himself nor through human beings
p: The phrase echoes Paul's claim for his own apostleship in Galatians 1:1.
b: Greek ouk aph' heautou oude di' anthrōpōn. Paul calls himself 'an apostle: not an apostle from people, and not through any human being, but through Jesus Christ and God the Father' (Galatians 1:1). Lightfoot calls the line 'An obvious reflexion' of that verse: 'Neither did he himself originate (ἀπό), nor did other men confer (διά), the office.' Lightfoot also reads 'the love of God' as God's love that 'conferred the office upon him'. Read beside 1:0, Ignatius holds both that the officers were 'appointed' by people and that their ministry comes from God.
orig: οὐκ ἀφ᾽ ἑαυτοῦ οὐδὲ δι᾽ ἀνθρώπων

a: to puff himself up
p: Ignatius uses half of Philippians 2:3 here and the other half at 8:2.
b: Greek oude kata kenodoxian, 'nor according to empty glory'. Paul wrote mēden kat' eritheian mēde kata kenodoxian: 'Do nothing to push yourselves forward or to puff yourselves up' (Philippians 2:3). Ignatius uses the second phrase of the overseer here and the first at 8:2 ('do nothing to push yourselves forward'). Lightfoot points out the pair. The Plain English Translation uses the site's wording of Philippians in both places so the reader sees it.

a: I am amazed at his forbearance
p: Greek epieikeia, 'forbearance': a quality meant to reassure, yet it 'strikes' Ignatius.
b: Greek hou katapeplēgmai tēn epieikeian. Epieikeia is 'forbearance', as in 1 Clement and Ignatius to the Ephesians 10:3. Lightfoot sees 'an oxymoron' here: katapeplēgmai means to be struck with awe, 'since ἐπιείκεια is the quality to reassure, not to dismay'. Lightfoot also notes that 'Ignatius had passed through Philadelphia on his way to Smyrna'; 'I know' (egnōn) is first-hand.

a: by keeping silent he can do more
p: As at Ephesus, Ignatius praises a quiet overseer.
b: Ignatius says the same of the overseer of Ephesus: 'the more anyone sees the overseer keeping silent, the more he should fear him' (Ignatius to the Ephesians 6:1). Lightfoot sees a second paradox beside 'amazed at his forbearance': here 'silence is said to be more eloquent than speech'. The letter does not say who 'those who talk emptily' were, or whether anyone had held the overseer's silence against him; it says only that Ignatius thinks his silence worth more than their talk.
r: Ignatius to the Ephesians 6:1; Ignatius to the Ephesians 15:1-2; James 1:19

a: as a lyre is to its strings
p: Ignatius uses the lyre again, but here the picture runs the other way from Ephesians 4:1.
b: Greek synerrythmistai gar tais entolais hōs chordais kithara, 'he is tuned together with the commandments as a lyre with strings'. In Ignatius to the Ephesians 4:1 the council of elders is fitted to the overseer 'as strings are to a lyre'. Here the overseer is the lyre and the commandments the strings. Lightfoot finds the picture unclear ('It is not easy to see in what sense the harp as a whole can be said to harmonize with the several strings') and wonders whether to read 'strings to a lyre', as the Armenian may have; the Greek and Latin have the order Lake prints. He adds that the verb seems to occur nowhere else.
orig: συνευρύθμισται γὰρ ταῖς ἐντολαῖς ὡς χορδαῖς κιθάρα

a: his steadiness and his freedom from anger
p: Lightfoot: here Ignatius 'runs into Stoic phraseology'.
b: Greek to akinēton autou kai to aorgēton, 'his unmovedness and his not-being-angry', with enareton, 'virtuous', before them. Lightfoot: enaretos is not in the Septuagint or the New Testament but 'a favourite word with the Stoics', and 'Ignatius here runs into Stoic phraseology'. Lake renders 'the unmoveable and passionless temper'. Lightfoot also thinks 'living' might belong with the overseer rather than with God, as the Armenian suggests; the Plain English Translation follows the Greek order, 'the living God'.
orig: τὸ ἀκίνητον αὐτοῦ καὶ τὸ ἀόργητον αὐτοῦ

a: Where the shepherd is
p: The overseer as shepherd and the false teachers as wolves, the picture of John 10 and Acts 20.
b: Greek hopou de ho poimēn estin, ekei hōs probata akoloutheite. Ignatius pictures the overseer as shepherd. Paul warned the elders of Ephesus, whom he also calls overseers, 'vicious wolves will get in among you and show the flock no mercy' (Acts 20:29), and Jesus warned against false prophets who 'come to you dressed up as sheep, but underneath they are wolves out for prey' (Matthew 7:15). In the Gospel the Good Shepherd is Christ (John 10:11); Ignatius applies the picture to the local overseer, as 1 Peter 5:2-4 does to elders under 'the chief shepherd'.

a: God's runners
p: Greek theodromoi, 'God-runners': Christians running the race God has set.
b: Greek tous theodromous. Lake: 'the runners in God's race'. Lightfoot: 'the runners in the stadium of God', 'the metaphor of the Christian δρόμος, which occurs so frequently in S. Paul', and he compares 'Your run was going well. Who cut in front of you?' (Galatians 5:7). The same word comes back in Ignatius to Polycarp 7:2 in another sense, of the messenger to be sent to Syria; Lightfoot there renders 'God's courier'.

a: the evil weeds
p: The picture echoes Jesus's words in Matthew 15:13.
b: Greek tōn kakōn botanōn, hastinas ou geōrgei Iēsous Christos, dia to mē einai autous phyteian patros. Lake's margin gives Matthew 15:13: 'Any plant that was not planted by my heavenly Father will be uprooted.' Lightfoot also hears the weeds sown by the enemy (Matthew 13:24-30) and the Father as farmer (John 15:1; 1 Corinthians 3:9). The 'weeds' are people: the pronoun 'they' is masculine, Lightfoot notes, as in the same picture in To the Trallians 11. Ignatius used botanē for the devil's 'weed' in Ignatius to the Ephesians 10:3.
r: Matthew 15:13; Matthew 13:24-30; John 15:1; 1 Corinthians 3:9; Ignatius to the Ephesians 10:3

a: Not that I found division among you
p: The church had strained the false teachers out, rather than split.
b: Greek ouch hoti par' hymin merismon heuron, all' apodiylismon. The noun is from diylizō, 'strain', the verb of 'filtering out the gnat' (Matthew 23:24). Lake's footnote: 'The meaning is that the Christians at Philadelphia had "filtered out" the impurity of heresy from their church.' Lightfoot: the believers 'had separated themselves from the heretics; but this separation deserved the name of "filtering," rather than of "division"'. He compares Ignatius to the Romans 1:0, 'filtered clean of every foreign stain'. 'I found' shows Ignatius had been there.
orig: οὐχ ὅτι παρ᾽ ὑμῖν μερισμὸν εὗρον, ἀλλ᾽ ἀποδιϋλισμόν

a: all who repent and come to the unity of the church
p: Ignatius leaves a door open: those who repent and come back belong to God.
b: Greek hosoi an metanoēsantes elthōsin epi tēn henotēta tēs ekklēsias. Beside his warnings (3:3), Ignatius promises a welcome for any who repent; he says the same at 8:1. The Catholic Encyclopedia (1910) lists 3 among the places that teach that 'the Church was Divinely established as a visible society, the salvation of souls is its end, and those who separate themselves from it cut themselves off from God', and says that here Ignatius 'denounces in principle the Protestant doctrine of private judgment in matters of religion'. Lightfoot reads the chapter of a particular group at Philadelphia that had left the church's meal and set up its own (see 4:1). On what makes the church one, see the topic The Church and the card on the Ephesians book page.
orig: ὅσοι ἂν μετανοήσαντες ἔλθωσιν ἐπὶ τὴν ἑνότητα τῆς ἐκκλησίας

a: Do not be deceived, my brothers
p: Ignatius borrows Paul's warning and his words 'will not inherit the kingdom of God'.
b: Paul: 'Or do you not know that the unrighteous will not inherit the kingdom of God? Do not be deceived' (1 Corinthians 6:9); and after the list of sins, 'will inherit the kingdom of God' (1 Corinthians 6:10). Lake's margin gives these verses; Lightfoot says the phrase 'is clearly suggested by 1 Cor. vi. 9 sq'. Ignatius changes two things: Paul's future 'will not inherit' becomes the present 'does not inherit', and Paul's list of sins becomes one sin, following a maker of splits. He made the same borrowing at Ignatius to the Ephesians 16:1.
r: 1 Corinthians 6:9-10; Galatians 5:20-21; Ignatius to the Ephesians 16:1

a: a maker of splits
p: Greek schizon, 'one who splits': the verb behind 'schism'.
b: Greek ei tis schizonti akolouthei. The participle of schizō, 'split', is the verb of schisma, which the Plain English Translation renders 'split' (the site's Galatians 5:20 has 'splits'). Lightfoot: 'making a rent, causing a schism', an absolute use he does not find in the Septuagint or the New Testament. Lake: 'a maker of schism'.

a: he does not agree with the suffering
p: Greek synkatatithetai, 'cast in one's vote with'; Lake: 'he has no part in the Passion'.
b: Greek houtos tō pathei ou synkatatithetai. Lightfoot: 'has no part or agreement with, dissociates himself from', a vote-casting word ('to cast in one's vote or lot with'), used of Joseph of Arimathea, who 'had not agreed' with the council (Luke 23:51). He reads it of the separate meal: 'By thus severing themselves from the true eucharist of the Church, they severed themselves from the passion of Christ.' 'The suffering' is Christ's, as in Ignatius to the Smyrnaeans 5:3.

a: one thanksgiving
p: Greek eucharistia: here the church's meal of bread and cup. Lake: 'one Eucharist'.
b:
Greek mia eucharistia chrēsthai. The Plain English Translation keeps 'thanksgiving' for eucharistia in every book, so the reader can follow the one Greek word from the Didache into Ignatius; here, as in Ignatius to the Smyrnaeans 7:1 and 8:1, it plainly names the church's meal, and Lake translates 'Eucharist'. Lightfoot counts these passages of Ignatius among 'the earliest instances of εὐχαριστία applied to the Holy Communion', with perhaps the Didache.

The 'one flesh' and 'one cup' echo Lake's margin, 1 Corinthians 10:16-17: 'The cup of blessing that we bless: is it not a sharing in the blood of Christ? ... Because there is one loaf, we who are many are one body.' Lightfoot: 'The "one flesh" here is the one eucharistic loaf betokening the union in the one body of Christ.'
r: 1 Corinthians 10:16-17; 1 Corinthians 11:20-26; Didache 9:4; Ignatius to the Smyrnaeans 7:1

a: There is one altar
t: One altar, one overseer: how it is read
p: What 'one altar' means, and how the churches read the verse.
b:
Greek hen thysiastērion, hōs heis episkopos. 'Altar' is the word of Ignatius to the Ephesians 5:2 ('within the altar'). Lightfoot thinks it 'would be an anachronism to suppose that Ignatius by the "altar" here means the "Lord's table"'; he takes it, as at Ephesians 5, of the gathered church at prayer, and sets beside it Cyprian's later 'one altar and one priesthood'.

Catholic teaching reads the verse as a witness to Christ's presence in the Eucharist: Joseph Pohle's article in the Catholic Encyclopedia (1909) lists 'Philadelphians 4' among the fathers who 'attest without the slightest shadow of a misunderstanding' the Real Presence. The commemoration page of the Southern District of the Lutheran Church—Missouri Synod says that in his letters Ignatius stressed 'the reality of Christ's bodily presence in the Lord's Supper'; it speaks of the letters in general, not of this verse. Lightfoot reads the stress on 'one' as aimed at a rival meal. The cards on Christ's presence in the Supper (Exodus 1-15; John 6), on who may lead it (Ignatius to the Smyrnaeans 8) and on how often (Acts 20:7) set out the churches' answers. No Orthodox, Reformed or Baptist document discussing this verse was opened for this note, so none is cited here.
r: Ignatius to the Ephesians 5:2; Ignatius to the Smyrnaeans 8:1; 1 Corinthians 10:18-21; Hebrews 13:10; John 6:53-56

a: my fellow slaves
p: Ignatius, an overseer himself, calls the deacons his fellow slaves.
b: Greek tois syndoulois mou, as he calls the deacon Burrhus 'my fellow slave' in Ignatius to the Ephesians 2:1. The word is the one Paul uses of Epaphras and Tychicus (Colossians 1:7; Colossians 4:7).
r: Colossians 1:7; Colossians 4:7; Ignatius to the Ephesians 2:1

a: I am pouring myself out in love for you
p: Greek ekkechymai, 'I am poured out': lavish affection.
b: Greek lian ekkechymai agapōn hymas. Lightfoot: the word implies 'profuse demonstrations of love'. Then asphalizomai hymas: Lightfoot 'I warn you, put you on your guard'; Lake 'watching over your safety'. Ignatius at once corrects himself: 'Yet it is not I, but Jesus Christ', the turn of Galatians 2:20.

a: I may reach the lot in which I was shown mercy
p: The 'lot' is the martyrdom God's mercy has set before him.
b: Greek hina en hō klērō ēleēthēn epitychō. The verb is the one the Plain English Translation renders 'reach' in 'reach God' (Ignatius to the Romans 1:2); here its object is 'the lot'. Lightfoot: the lot is 'Of martyrdom', and the sense is 'that I may secure, make good, the lot, in which ... God's mercy placed me'. 'Shown mercy' is Paul's way of speaking of his own calling (1 Timothy 1:13, 16).
r: 1 Timothy 1:13-16; 2 Corinthians 4:1; Ignatius to the Romans 1:1-2

a: in the gospel as in the flesh of Jesus
t: The gospel as Christ's flesh, the apostles as elders
p: Is Ignatius speaking of written books, the Gospels and the apostles' letters, or of the message?
b:
Greek prosphygōn tō euangeliō hōs sarki Iēsou, kai tois apostolois hōs presbyteriō ekklēsias. The gospel gives Ignatius Christ's earthly life, and the apostles stand to the whole church as each church's elders stand to it (Lightfoot). Lightfoot calls the picture 'eucharistic', perhaps with a hint against those who denied Christ's flesh.

Whether books are meant is argued. Lightfoot: the words point 'to some authoritative writings of the New Testament'; Ussher, Pearson, Leclerc, Westcott and Hilgenfeld took 'the gospel' as the Gospels and 'the apostles' as the apostles' letters, while Zahn and others took 'the gospel' as the message. Lightfoot leans to Zahn: 'the idea of written documents is not intended in the word εὐαγγέλιον itself, but only involved in the subsequent mention of the "Apostles"'. See also 8:2 and 9:2.
orig: προσφυγὼν τῷ εὐαγγελίῳ ὡς σαρκὶ Ἰησοῦ

a: We love the prophets too
p: Lake thinks of Christian prophets; Lightfoot of the prophets of Israel.
b:
Greek kai tous prophētas de agapōmen. Lake's two footnotes: 'He probably means the Christian prophets: cf. the Didache and Hermas', and 'An alternative translation is "let us love."' Lightfoot takes the verb as a statement, 'we love', not 'let us love', and the prophets as Israel's: they 'foretold the Gospel and awaited the coming of Christ', and the line answers Judaizers. Its sense: 'We do not disparage the prophets any more than yourselves; only we maintain the superiority of the Gospel.' He links it to 9:1-2.

'By believing in him they were saved': Lightfoot reads this, with To the Magnesians 9, of Christ's going to the dead (see the topic on Christ's descent).

a: the hope we share
p: Lightfoot: 'our common hope' is Christ, as in 11:2.
b: Greek tēs koinēs elpidos. Lightfoot: the hope is 'Christ, as appears from § 11 below' ('Farewell in Christ Jesus, the hope we share'). The word 'common' fits the point of the verse, he says: 'all alike, whether they lived before or after the coming of Christ, are united in a common Saviour.'

a: do not listen to him
p: Whom does Ignatius mean? Lightfoot thinks of Gentile Christians teaching Jewish practice from the prophets.
b:
Greek ean de tis ioudaismon hermēneuē hymin. 'Judaism' is the word of Galatians 1:13 ('when I was in Judaism'), and 'Christianity' the word of Ignatius to the Romans 3:3. Lightfoot: hermēneuein here names the result of interpreting, so that someone reads the prophets of 5:2 'so as to support Judaizing practices'. He thinks the uncircumcised teacher is the same person, 'Gentile Christians with strong Judaic tendencies', since 'the effective proselytizing of Jews and Judaic Christians among persons of Gentile origin is a patent fact'.

So the line is about Christians, not about the Jewish people: a circumcised man who teaches Christ is better than an uncircumcised one who teaches 'Judaism'. Lake's introduction says 'it is disputed' whether these Judaizers belonged to the same circles as the docetists; the Catholic Encyclopedia's article on the Docetae holds that in Ignatius's day 'Docetism seems to have been closely connected with Judaism', citing chapters 6 and 8. See the topics on the Judaizers and on anti-Judaism.
orig: Ἐὰν δέ τις ἰουδαϊσμὸν ἑρμηνεύῃ ὑμῖν
r: Galatians 1:13-14; Galatians 2:14; Galatians 6:12-15; Ignatius to the Romans 3:3; Ignatius to the Magnesians 10:3

a: if neither of them speaks
p: The Greek says 'if both do not speak': the warning covers both teachers.
b: Greek ean de amphoteroi peri Iēsou Christou mē lalōsin, 'but if both do not speak about Jesus Christ'. 'Both' are the two teachers just named, the circumcised man and the uncircumcised one. The Plain English Translation says 'neither of them' because in English 'if both do not speak' could mean 'if not both speak'. Ignatius's point is that either teacher, whatever his birth, is a grave marker if he does not speak of Christ.
orig: ἐὰν δὲ ἀμφότεροι περὶ Ἰησοῦ Χριστοῦ μὴ λαλῶσιν

a: grave markers and tombs of the dead
p: Teachers who never speak of Christ are like grave markers: a name, and nothing alive.
b: Greek stēlai eisin kai taphoi nekrōn, eph' hois gegraptai monon onomata anthrōpōn. A stēlē was the upright stone over a grave with the dead person's name cut in it. Lightfoot paraphrases: 'they are no better than tombstones inscribed with men's names', and compares Jesus's 'tombs painted with whitewash' (Matthew 23:27). The words apply to both teachers of the verse, circumcised or not, if they 'do not speak about Jesus Christ'.

a: It is better to hear Christianity from a circumcised man
p: The test for Ignatius is what is taught, not who teaches it.
b: Greek ameinon gar estin para andros peritomēn echontos christianismon akouein, ē para akrobystou ioudaismon. The verse does not belittle Jewish believers: it says a Jewish Christian who teaches Christ is to be heard. Revelation's letter to the same city speaks of 'the synagogue of Satan, who say they are Jews and are not' (Revelation 3:9); Lightfoot connects the two, holding that Philadelphia 'was a stronghold of the Jews' and that the letter controverts 'a stubborn form of Judaism'. Revelation 3:9 is about a synagogue, Ignatius about teachers in the church; any link between them is Lightfoot's inference.
orig: παρὰ ἀνδρὸς περιτομὴν ἔχοντος χριστιανισμὸν ἀκούειν

a: the ruler of this age
p: Ignatius's name for Satan, as in Ignatius to the Ephesians 17:1 and 19:1.
b: Greek tou archontos tou aiōnos toutou. Paul speaks of 'the rulers of this age' (1 Corinthians 2:6, 8); John has 'the ruler of this world' (John 12:31). His 'evil arts' (kakotechniai) and 'traps' are the false teaching of the chapter. The same 'evil arts' are named in Ignatius to Polycarp 5:1.
r: 1 Corinthians 2:6-8; John 12:31; Ephesians 6:11; Ignatius to the Ephesians 17:1

a: I was a burden to anyone
p: Ignatius defends his stay, as Paul defended his.
b: Greek hoti ebarēsa tina en mikrō ē en megalō. Lightfoot compares 2 Corinthians 11:9: 'When I was with you and ran short, I was a weight on no one.' Paul says the same to the Thessalonians (1 Thessalonians 2:9). The verse shows Ignatius had stayed at Philadelphia and that some said hard things about his visit (7:1-2).

a: it knows where it comes from and where it is going
p: Ignatius takes up Jesus's words about the wind and the Spirit.
b: Greek oiden gar, pothen erchetai kai pou hypagei. Jesus: 'The wind blows where it wants to. You hear the sound of it, yet where it comes from and where it is going you do not know. That is how it is with everyone born from the Spirit' (John 3:8). Lake's margin gives the verse; Lightfoot: 'The coincidence is quite too strong to be accidental', and the Gospel is 'prior'. Ignatius turns it around: no one else knows the Spirit's movements, but the Spirit knows them. 'Exposes what is hidden' recalls 1 Corinthians 2:10 (Lake's margin) and 1 Corinthians 14:24-25.
orig: οἶδεν γάρ, πόθεν ἔρχεται καὶ ποῦ ὑπάγει

a: some people wanted to deceive me in the flesh
p: Some at Philadelphia tried to mislead Ignatius; he does not say how.
b: Greek ei gar kai kata sarka me tines ēthelēsan planēsai. Lightfoot: 'It is vain to speculate on the circumstance to which Ignatius alludes'; 'in the flesh' suggests 'some deceit practised upon him ... in the common affairs of life', which could not touch the Spirit. He adds: 'The obscurity of the allusion is a strong testimony to the genuineness of the letter.' Lightfoot takes 'the Spirit' as 'the Spirit which is working in me'.
orig: κατὰ σάρκα μέ τινες ἠθέλησαν πλανῆσαι

a: I cried out while I was among you
t: A prophet's cry in the assembly
p: Ignatius says he spoke with 'the voice of God' at Philadelphia: prophecy in the church.
b:
Greek ekraugasa metaxy ōn, elaloun megalē phōnē, theou phōnē. While he was among them, Ignatius spoke out as a prophet, and the words were the Spirit's (7:2). Lightfoot compares Jesus's 'loud voice' at Lazarus's tomb (John 11:43) and 1 Clement 59:1, where the writer makes a like claim for what God 'has said through us'. He rejects Bunsen's view that the 'cry' was a letter: the context shows Ignatius 'had himself visited Philadelphia'.

Prophecy in the gathering is found in 1 Corinthians 14 and Acts 13:2. That the Spirit's message was 'Pay attention to the overseer' shows how closely Ignatius joins prophecy and church order. On prophecy in the churches today, see the card at Ephesians 2:20.

a: Some suspected that I said this
p: The Greek leaves the sentence hanging: 'those who suspected me ...'.
b: Greek hoi de hypopteusantes me hōs proeidota ton merismon tinōn legein tauta, 'but those who suspected me as knowing beforehand ... to say these things'. The sentence has no main verb. Lightfoot calls it an anacoluthon, a sentence left unfinished 'in the hurry of dictating', and notes that the Greek manuscript G has a corrupt ptesantes for hypopteusantes, while the Latin translates literally and the Syriac and Armenian straightened the syntax. The Plain English Translation gives the sense: they suspected that a human informant had told him.
orig: οἱ δὲ ὑποπτεύσαντές με ὡς προειδότα

a: I did not learn it from human flesh
p: As Peter's confession was not revealed by 'flesh and blood'.
b: Greek hoti apo sarkos anthrōpinēs ouk egnōn. Lightfoot points to Matthew 16:17: 'flesh and blood did not uncover this for you. My Father in heaven did.' Paul says his gospel came 'not from a human being' (Galatians 1:12). Lightfoot rejects the claim that an apocryphal book is quoted here: 'Ignatius is plainly speaking throughout this passage of a spiritual revelation'.

a: Keep your flesh as God's temple
p: A short form of Paul's teaching that the believer's body is a temple.
b: Greek tēn sarka hymōn hōs naon theou tēreite. Paul: 'your body is a temple of the Holy Spirit within you' (1 Corinthians 6:19; compare 1 Corinthians 3:16). 2 Clement 9:3 has nearly the same words, 'So we must guard the flesh as a temple of God' (Lightfoot). The Spirit's five commands sum up the letter: the overseer, the body, union, no divisions, the imitation of Christ.
orig: τὴν σάρκα ὑμῶν ὡς ναὸν θεοῦ τηρεῖτε

a: the council of the overseer
p: Greek synedrion, the word for the Jewish council: the overseer with his elders.
b: Greek synedrion tou episkopou. Lightfoot: 'the bishop with his council of presbyters as assessors'; he notes a civic 'council of elders' at Philadelphia in an inscription. In the Gospels synedrion is the high council at Jerusalem (Mark 14:55). Ignatius pictures the elders seated round their overseer (To the Magnesians 6:1).

a: who will loosen every bond from you
p: Perhaps an echo of Isaiah 58:6, a favorite verse of the early church.
b: Greek hos lysei aph' hymōn panta desmon. Lightfoot notes the long recension replaced 'bond' with the words of Isaiah 58:6 in the Greek (the site's Isaiah 58:6 from the Hebrew: 'to unlock the fetters of wickedness'), and that the verse 'seems to have been a very favourite citation in the early Church'. Whether Ignatius alludes to it 'may or may not' be so; he takes the bond to be 'the power of evil generally'. Hilgenfeld, he reports, saw 'the oppressive yoke of Judaism'.

a: the way of learning Christ
p: Greek christomathia, 'Christ-learning', a rare compound.
b: Greek kata christomathian. The word joins 'Christ' and the root of 'learn' and 'disciple'. Lightfoot finds the related christomathēs in a much later writer (Modestus); he compares Ignatius's own christonomos, 'named after Christ' (Ignatius to the Romans 1:0). Lake: 'after the teaching of Christ'. Paul has the verb: 'But that is not how you learned Christ' (Ephesians 4:20).

a: I heard some people say
t: The archives, the gospel and 'It is written'
p: The most argued sentence of the letter: what were 'the archives', and how should it be punctuated?
b:
Greek ean mē en tois archeiois heurō en tō euangeliō ou pisteuō, with no punctuation. Lake's footnote gives two ways to divide it and prefers 'If I find it not in the charters,—in the Gospel I do not believe', since 'the charters' probably means the Old Testament: the common reading, 'I do not believe in the gospel'. Lightfoot says the passage is 'almost universally taken' that way, 'with the very rare construction which occurs Mark i. 15', but argues for his own: 'Unless I find it (the point at issue) in the archives, I do not believe it (because it appears) in the Gospel. The parallelism demands this.' He rejects Zahn's 'in the archives, that is, in the Gospel'.

The Plain English Translation follows Lightfoot, not Lake, for those two reasons. The long recension and the Armenian ('I do not believe the gospel') show that some early readers took it the common way. On every reading the objectors accept nothing they cannot find in 'the archives'. See the deep notes at chapter 8.
orig: ἐὰν μὴ ἐν τοῖς ἀρχείοις εὕρω ἐν τῷ εὐαγγελίῳ οὐ πιστεύω

a: That is the question
p: Greek prokeitai, 'it lies before us': the point in dispute.
b: Greek apekrithēsan moi hoti prokeitai. Lightfoot: 'This is the question before us, this remains to be proved', with examples from many writers; he dismisses other renderings ('It stands already written', 'It is obvious') as 'forcing a meaning on πρόκειται which is alien to it'. Lake: 'that is exactly the question'. The opponents grant that the words are written but deny that they mean what Ignatius says: the dispute is about interpretation.

a: to me Jesus Christ is the archives
t: Christ, the archives no one can tamper with
p: Ignatius's last word in the debate: Christ's cross and resurrection are the record that settles it.
b:
Greek emoi de archeia estin Iēsous Christos, ta athikta archeia ho stauros autou kai ho thanatos kai hē anastasis autou kai hē pistis hē di' autou. Lightfoot paraphrases: 'Jesus Christ is the archives; He contains in Himself the documentary proofs of His person and mission'. Athikta, 'not to be touched', was used 'of sacrosanct places', he notes.

Lightfoot reads the words as Ignatius setting the argument aside after joining it: 'Though I have condescended to argue ... yet to myself such an appeal is superfluous: Jesus Christ is the archives.' Zahn, as Lightfoot reports him, took the objectors to be appealing to the original documents of the New Testament, so that 'the gospel' would already be a written standard; Lightfoot rejects this (see the note on 'I heard some people say'). No church document discussing this verse was opened for these notes. The churches' views of Scripture and tradition are set side by side on the cards at Matthew 15, 2 Thessalonians 2:15 and 1 Timothy 3:15. The Catholic Encyclopedia's article on Ignatius cites chapter 3, not this verse, for his teaching on the church.
orig: ἐμοὶ δὲ ἀρχεῖά ἐστιν Ἰησοῦς Χριστός
r: John 5:39-40; John 5:46; Luke 24:27; 2 Thessalonians 2:15; 1 Timothy 3:15; Matthew 15:3

a: In these I want to be justified
p: Ignatius uses Paul's word: justified, through the cross and resurrection and faith.
b: Greek en hois thelō en tē proseuchē hymōn dikaiōthēnai. 'Justify' is the site's rendering of dikaioō in Paul (Romans 5:1; Galatians 2:16). Lightfoot compares Romans 5 (Ignatius to the Romans 5:1: 'I am not justified by that'), on his sufferings. What justifies is 'his cross, his death, his resurrection, and the faith that comes through him'.
r: Romans 5:1; Galatians 2:16; Romans 4:25; Ignatius to the Romans 5:1

a: The priests are good too, but better is the high priest
t: The priests and the high priest
p: The priests of Israel are good; Christ the high priest is better, as in Hebrews.
b:
Greek kaloi kai hoi hiereis, kreisson de ho archiereus. Lightfoot: 'The contrast here is between the Levitical priesthood, and the great High-priest of the Gospel'; the coincidences with Hebrews 'show, I think, that Ignatius must have had the Epistle to the Hebrews' in mind. The high priest alone entered the most holy place (Hebrews 9:7); 'the hidden things of God' are, Lightfoot suggests, what the ark held.

The long recension rewrote the verse to speak of the Christian ministry ('the priests and the ministers of the word'), making 'high priest' the bishop; Lightfoot says Cotelier was misled by it. In the short text the high priest is Christ, who is also 'the Father's door'.
orig: Καλοὶ καὶ οἱ ἱερεῖς, κρεῖσσον δὲ ὁ ἀρχιερεύς

a: He himself is the Father's door
p: Christ the door, as in John 10:9; the open door of Revelation 3:8 was promised to this same church.
b: Greek autos ōn thyra tou patros. Jesus: 'I am the door. Whoever goes in through me will be rescued' (John 10:9). Lightfoot notes 'this image occurs in the message to the Philadelphian Church': 'Look, I have set an open door in front of you' (Revelation 3:8). Through this door come Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, the prophets, the apostles and the church: all who are saved come to the Father through Christ, before his coming and after (5:2; John 14:6).

a: the coming of the Savior
p: Greek parousia, usually Christ's coming at the end; here his coming in the flesh.
b: Greek tēn parousian tou sōtēros. The Plain English Translation renders parousia 'coming' throughout. Lightfoot: here 'The reference is obviously to the first advent, the incarnation, though the word, when not specially defined, generally refers to the second advent'; early writers such as Justin 'are careful to distinguish the two παρουσίαι of Christ'.

a: the gospel is the completion of incorruption
p: The gospel completes what the prophets began: life that cannot decay.
b: Greek to de euangelion apartisma estin aphtharsias. Lightfoot: 'the completed work of immortality, as the law was the first stage', the word matching 'brought to completion' in Ignatius to the Smyrnaeans 7:2. Aphtharsia, 'incorruption', is the eternal life the gospel gives, with 'the idea of moral incorruption'. Compare 2 Timothy 1:10, where through the good news Christ 'has brought life and immortality out into the light' (Greek aphtharsia there too).
r: 2 Timothy 1:10; 1 Corinthians 15:53-54; Ignatius to the Smyrnaeans 7:2

a: the church in Antioch of Syria is at peace
p: News that Ignatius's own church was at peace reached him after he left Smyrna.
b: Greek eirēneuein tēn ekklēsian tēn en Antiocheia tēs Syrias. From Smyrna Ignatius had asked prayer for the church in Syria (Ignatius to the Ephesians 21:2). Lightfoot: by the time he reached Troas 'he had heard that the persecution was ended', and 'in the three letters written from thence he charges his readers to send delegates' (Ignatius to the Smyrnaeans 11:2; Ignatius to Polycarp 7:1-2). He thinks Philo and Rheus Agathopus (11:1) brought the news. Lightfoot also links 'in answer to your prayer' with 'is at peace', not with 'news has reached me'.
orig: εἰρηνεύειν τὴν ἐκκλησίαν τὴν ἐν Ἀντιοχείᾳ τῆς Συρίας
r: Ignatius to the Smyrnaeans 11:1-3; Ignatius to Polycarp 7:1; Acts 11:19-26

a: as a church of God
p: Greek cheirotonesai, a word for choosing that first meant voting with a raised hand: the whole church chooses.
b: Greek prepon estin hymin hōs ekklēsia theou, cheirotonēsai diakonon. The Tyndale House brief lexicon (after Abbott-Smith) gives its first sense as 'to vote by stretching out the hand in the Athenian ἐκκλησία', then 'to appoint', by vote at 2 Corinthians 8:19 and without one at Acts 14:23. The site renders it 'chose' in Acts 14:23 ('They chose elders for them in each church') and 'voted' in 2 Corinthians 8:19 ('the churches voted for him'), and 'elect' in Ignatius to the Smyrnaeans 11:2. Here it is the church, 'as a church of God', that chooses. Lightfoot: the envoy 'to Syria, as their representative' is called 'God's ambassador' here, 'God-ambassador' in Ignatius to the Smyrnaeans 11:2 and 'God's runner' in Ignatius to Polycarp 7:2.
r: Acts 14:23; 2 Corinthians 8:19; Ignatius to the Smyrnaeans 11:2; Ignatius to Polycarp 7:2

a: the nearest churches have sent overseers
p: Some churches sent their overseer to Antioch, others elders and deacons.
b: Greek hōs kai hai engista ekklēsiai epempsan episkopous, hai de presbyterous kai diakonous. The verse says only that some nearby churches sent overseers and others elders and deacons. Lightfoot guesses the 'others' were churches 'not so near and whose bishop could not be spared'. It shows the three offices by name and churches caring for one another across provinces. On the offices see the cards at 1 Timothy 3, Acts 20:28 and Philippians 1:1.
r: 2 Corinthians 8:18-23; Acts 15:22; Ignatius to the Smyrnaeans 11:2

a: Philo, the deacon from Cilicia
p: Two companions who followed Ignatius from the east, through Philadelphia and Smyrna to Troas.
b: Ignatius names the same two in Ignatius to the Smyrnaeans 10:1: 'Philo and Rheus Agathopus followed me for the word of God'. Lightfoot: they 'had followed in the track of Ignatius', passing through Philadelphia and Smyrna, and reached him at Troas, and were probably 'the bearers of the good news that the persecution at Antioch had ceased'. The Catholic Encyclopedia says a later account of his martyrdom is 'reputed to have been written by Philo, deacon of Tarsus, and Rheus Agathopus'. 'Has said goodbye to this life' is Lake's 'has renounced this life'.
orig: Περὶ δὲ Φίλωνος τοῦ διακόνου ἀπὸ Κιλικίας
r: Ignatius to the Smyrnaeans 10:1; Acts 21:39; Acts 15:41

a: as the Lord also welcomed you
p: Lake's footnote allows a wish instead: 'even as may the Lord receive you'.
b: Greek hōs kai hymas ho kyrios, with no verb. Lake supplies the past, 'even as the Lord received you', and his footnote adds: 'Or possibly "even as may the Lord receive you."' Compare Romans 15:7: 'So welcome one another, just as Christ welcomed you'.

a: may those who dishonored them be redeemed
p: Some at Philadelphia had snubbed Ignatius's companions; he prays for them.
b: Greek hoi de atimasantes autous lytrōtheiēsan. Lightfoot thinks the two men 'received a hearty welcome from the main body of the church; but some persons—doubtless his Judaizing opponents—had treated them with contempt', and that from them Ignatius heard of the charges against his own stay (6:3; 7:2). He answers with a prayer, as he asks prayer for the opponents in Ignatius to the Smyrnaeans 4:1.
r: Luke 6:28; Romans 12:14; Ignatius to the Smyrnaeans 4:1

a: the brothers in Troas
p: Eusebius: from Troas Ignatius wrote to Philadelphia, to Smyrna and to Polycarp.
b: Eusebius, Church History 3.36.10: 'when he was already past Smyrna, from Troas he again addressed in writing those in Philadelphia, and the church of the Smyrnaeans, and in particular Polycarp, who led it' (the site's translation of the Greek). Troas, the port facing Macedonia, is where Paul saw the man of Macedonia (Acts 16:8-11) and where he broke bread on the first day of the week (Acts 20:6-12).
r: Acts 16:8-11; Acts 20:5-12; 2 Corinthians 2:12; Ignatius to the Smyrnaeans 12:1

a: by Burrhus
p: The Ephesian deacon who stayed with Ignatius, writing or carrying the letters from Troas.
b: Ignatius had asked that Burrhus, 'my fellow slave ... your deacon', stay with him (Ignatius to the Ephesians 2:1); Ignatius to the Smyrnaeans 12:1 is sent 'by Burrhus' too. Lightfoot: at Troas, 'Burrhus the Ephesian, alone of the delegates who had been with him at Smyrna, still remained in his company', and 'He was the amanuensis' (the one who wrote down the letter). 'By Burrhus' may mean by his hand as writer or as carrier.
r: Ignatius to the Ephesians 2:1; Ignatius to the Smyrnaeans 12:1; Romans 16:22
